lesson.title: Factoring Polynomials: From Messy Sums to Clean Products

steps.say: Imagine you're selling phone cases at a school fundraiser. Your profit, in dollars, depends on how many cases you sell, and it's given by P of x equals three x squared minus twenty-seven x plus fifty-four, where x is the number of cases. The big question: at how many cases do you break even, meaning profit is exactly zero? You could plug in numbers and hope, but there's a smarter path. If you can rewrite that messy expression as a product of simpler pieces, then by the zero-product rule, you just set each piece to zero and solve. That is exactly what factoring gives you. Turn a hard sum into an easy product, and the zeros pop out instantly.

visual.caption: The parabola crosses the x-axis at x = 3 and x = 6 — those are the break-even points

steps.say: Step one of factoring is always the same, no matter how scary the polynomial looks: pull out the greatest common factor. Look at your three terms — three x squared, minus twenty-seven x, plus fifty-four. What is the biggest whole number that divides all three coefficients? Three goes into three, into twenty-seven, into fifty-four. So you pull out a three, just like peeling a common layer off a bundle of sticks. You are left with three times the quantity x squared minus nine x plus eighteen. Notice: the GCF step does not change the answer, it just makes the next step cleaner.

visual.caption: The coefficient 3 is shared by all three terms — that is the GCF

steps.say: Now for the fun part: factor the trinomial x squared minus nine x plus eighteen. You are looking for two numbers, call them a and b, that multiply to the last term, eighteen, and add up to the middle coefficient, minus nine. Let's check the pairs: one times eighteen adds to nineteen, no good. Two times nine adds to eleven, nope. Three times six adds to nine — but we need minus nine. So try negative three and negative six: they multiply to positive eighteen, and they add to negative nine. Perfect. That means the trinomial splits into x minus three, times x minus six.

visual.caption: The pair (−3, −6) satisfies both conditions: product = 18, sum = −9

steps.say: Put it all together. Your profit expression is three, times x minus three, times x minus six. And here is the payoff: to find where profit equals zero, you set each factor to zero. Three is a constant, it never equals zero, so you skip it. x minus three equals zero gives x equals three. x minus six equals zero gives x equals six. In your fundraiser context, selling six cases covers all your costs. The root at three is a valid zero of the polynomial, but maybe below your minimum order. Either way, factoring turned a quadratic equation into two tiny one-step problems.

visual.caption: Same parabola, now written as a product — the zeros are obvious

steps.say: Let's meet a pattern you will use over and over: the difference of squares. If you have a perfect square minus another perfect square, like x squared minus twenty-five, that is x squared minus five squared. You can rewrite it as x minus five, times x plus five. Here is a way to see why: picture a big square with side length x, and cut out a smaller square of side five from one corner. The leftover L-shaped area can be sliced and rearranged into a single rectangle whose sides are x plus five and x minus five. Same area, different shape. That is the identity a squared minus b squared equals a minus b, times a plus b, and it works for any a and b, not just plain numbers.

visual.caption: With x = 7: a 7×7 square minus a 5×5 square leaves 49 − 25 = 24, exactly the area of a 12 by 2 rectangle, (x+5)(x−5)

steps.say: Let's do a slightly harder example to lock in the difference of squares. Factor four x squared minus nine. First, check for a GCF: four and nine share no factor other than one, so nothing to pull out. Now spot the pattern: four x squared is the same as two x, all squared, and nine is three squared. So this is a squared minus b squared with a equal to two x and b equal to three. The factorization is two x minus three, times two x plus three. Let's verify by expanding: two x times two x gives four x squared, two x times three gives six x, minus three times two x gives minus six x, and minus three times three gives minus nine. The middle terms cancel, leaving four x squared minus nine. It checks out.

Here is your one-line takeaway to carry into the next unit: factoring turns a hard 'sum equals zero' into an easy 'product equals zero,' and the zero-product rule does the rest. Always pull the GCF first, then look for the pattern — whether it is a trinomial you crack with two numbers, or a difference of squares you split with the a-minus-b, a-plus-b formula. Master those two moves and every polynomial in this course will feel like unpacking a gift you already know the answer to.

lesson.answer: Factoring turns 'sum equals zero' into 'product equals zero' — pull the GCF, spot the pattern, set each factor to zero, done.

practice.question: You're running a lemonade stand at a neighbourhood block party. Your profit in dollars from selling x cups is P(x) = 2x² − 16x + 30. (a) Factor the profit expression completely. (b) At how many cups do you break even (profit = 0)?
practice.answer: (a) P(x) = 2(x² − 8x + 15) = 2(x − 3)(x − 5). (b) Setting each factor to zero: x = 3 or x = 5. You break even after selling 3 cups or 5 cups.
